#### About William of Ockham

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) was an English Franciscan philosopher-theologian associated with late medieval nominalism.

### Interpretation

Ockham's principle is a methodological rule rather than a claim about the world. It says not to multiply entities beyond what explanation requires, so where a simpler account suffices, the additional postulate is unwarranted. It functions as a tie-breaker between theories rather than as proof that the simpler one is true. He applied it mainly to reject unnecessary metaphysical apparatus in his predecessors.

#### Why it matters

Used properly it chooses between adequate explanations, not between an explanation and none. It is often misused to dismiss the unfamiliar simply for being unfamiliar.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Plurality should not be posited without necessity.”?

“Plurality should not be posited without necessity.” comes from Summa Logicae et al., (principle), attributed to William of Ockham.

#### What does William of Ockham mean by reason?

Philosophers disagree about whether reason is the slave of the passions, the legislator of morality, or one tool among others. The quotations here keep that disagreement in play. This passage enters that discussion through reason, method.
